Coding was done by a single coder with no agreement statistic. The only check was an AI cross-read of three cells, which the paper concedes is not independent adjudication. Only 2 of the 3 flagged cells were reviewed against passages, and no complete passage-level sufficiency review of the other 42 decisions exists. Disagreements recorded in the change log (Opus 4.6 D2, Artifactory D4) were resolved by the primary coder in their own favour. Source-sufficiency is verified for only a few cells.

The direct/inferred split is an ad hoc mapping chosen by the study lead (class I means inferred, everything else direct). It is not a codebook category. The 36/5 split and the 'removing inferred support' column of Table III depend on it, and the column is almost redundant with the class-I count, so the analysis adds little.

The reported cell counts are partly artifacts of the coding scheme. For example, D2 'unknown' cells were recoded in round 7 by an analyst decision with no independent check. Table III's 'retained after removing single-source support' counts are driven by how many references were listed per cell, not by evidence strength. The paper itself notes that multiple references do not establish independence. Figure 1 and Table III therefore measure citation counts, not evidential support.

Novelty is incremental by the automated check, and the paper does not claim more. The cross-incident comparison is covered by prior work, and the comparison with that work is left as pending placeholders. The 'claim-support matrix' is mostly a 5×4 table of generic scope statements (Table II) and a codebook. It is not a demonstrated artifact with findings that go beyond the descriptive.

The ledger and bibliography are inconsistent. The R18 URL is 'not supplied', the bibliography itself notes that a locator correction is required, and R11–R17 and R19–R23 are 'not reauthenticated'. Many bibliography entries (e.g., Zenodo, SSRN and Research Square items on authorization and guardrails) are not cited in the text. The References section is only a stub sentence in the Markdown source.

The paper includes internal bookkeeping and process language, such as 'supplied aggregate records', 'supplied audit account' and 'the study lead'. This reads as a working-state report rather than a finished manuscript, which hurts clarity. Findings are hedged so heavily that RQ1–RQ4 receive few firm answers. The substantive result is that the comparison cannot yet be asserted.

The Appendix B table encodes status with ad hoc notation (U*, 'Review', 'D, unresolved') that differs from the three-valued codebook, so the 45-decision table cannot be tallied against the stated totals. Two of the 'unknown' cells are flagged as documented in the aggregates.
strengths: The paper states its inference boundaries openly: reachability is not permission, detection is not containment, and an attempt is not completion. These are useful distinctions for incident analysis and are applied consistently across the five dimensions.

The paper is candid about limitations. It declares single-coder coding, unresolved cells, dependent units and inaccessible sources, and it avoids prevalence or efficacy claims. The change log and audit trail make several recodings traceable.

Evidence classes (O/A/I/X) and the separation of replay results from live incident evidence are a sound way to handle heterogeneous documents. The point that separate authorship does not mean independent evidence is well taken.
The proposed minimum disclosure checklist is concrete and could be useful to evaluators, even though it has not been validated.
The paper has no experiments on real systems and adds no operational detail. The automated protocol check passed and the PDF is within the page limit.
